title: Who am I? (Exodus 3:11, 4:10–17)
hook: Moses protests that he is slow of speech; Aaron will speak for him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ehyeh: a name that is a verb, I will be what I will be. Your line was I will be what I will be. Today, that same word comes back as a promise to a man who doesn't want the job. Day eighty-three.
screen: `I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.`

segments.voice: Someone gets offered something big. A promotion, a speech at a wedding, a role they never imagined. And before they even think, the words come out: me? Oh, no. I'm not the right person. You'd be better off with someone else. Moses is standing at a burning bush, being told by God himself to go and free a nation of slaves. And he spends most of the conversation trying to get out of it. Today: ehyeh, I will be.
screen: `ME? I'M NOT THE RIGHT PERSON.` → `A BURNING BUSH, A HUGE JOB.` → `MOSES TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.`

segments.voice: His first objection is the biggest: "Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?" A shepherd. A fugitive. A man who ran away. And God's answer doesn't argue with him about who he is. God says: "Certainly I will be with thee." In Hebrew, ki ehyeh imach. There's yesterday's word. Ehyeh. I will be. The answer to who am I is: it's not only about you. Moses keeps going. What if they ask your name? What if they don't believe me? Each time, God answers. Then Moses gets personal: "I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." I'm not a speaker. Never have been. Nobody knows exactly what he means. A stammer? Rusty Hebrew after years in a palace, or rusty Egyptian after years in the desert? A midrash tells a story that as a baby in Pharaoh's house, he burned his tongue on a coal. The Torah doesn't explain. God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?" I'll be with your mouth. And finally Moses just says it: please, send someone else. And God is angry. The text says so. But God doesn't take the job away, and doesn't pretend the weakness isn't real. God says: your brother Aaron is coming to meet you, and he speaks well. He'll be your mouth, and you'll tell him what to say. So the man the Torah later calls a prophet like no other was a man who didn't think he could speak, and who needed his brother's help to do it. The weakness stayed. He was sent anyway, and not alone.
screen: `WHO AM I?` · `I WILL BE WITH THEE.` · `SLOW OF SPEECH, SLOW OF TONGUE.` · `AARON WILL BE YOUR MOUTH.` · then, large: `SLOW OF SPEECH, STILL SENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept help with a weakness. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're not good at, that keeps getting in your way. Speaking up. Numbers. Organizing. Asking for things. Don't argue it away. Name it honestly, the way Moses did. Then think: who's your Aaron? Who's good at this, and might help, if you asked? Picture asking them. The bell holds the time.
Ehyeh, I will be, God's answer to Moses' who am I: it's not about you, I will be with you.
Your line: slow of speech, still sent. Today, ask one person for help with something you're not good at. Day eighty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls Moses the greatest of the prophets and also the humblest of men, and teachers often point to his reluctance at the bush as part of why he was chosen.

match.prompt: Moses' objections and God's answers — tap the pairs.

myth: God took the job away when Moses objected
God was angry, but still sent him, with Aaron to help.
the Torah explains exactly what slow of speech means
it doesn't. a stammer, a forgotten language, a burned tongue in a midrash: nobody knows.
God's answer to who am I uses yesterday's word, ehyeh
ki ehyeh imach: I will be with thee.

fork.setup: you're God, speaking from the bush. the man you've chosen says he can't speak well and begs you to send someone else. what do you do?
options: send him anyway, with his brother to help.
heal his speech on the spot.
fork.reveal: God is angry, but sends him anyway: Aaron will be his mouth. the weakness stays, and Moses goes, not alone.

original.note: Hebrew: heavy of mouth, slow of speech. Moses' words about himself.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses was a born leader.
what it means: he argued his way through the whole call, and was sent anyway, with help.
what a scholar hears: k'vad peh, heavy of mouth. Exodus Rabbah 1:26 tells of the burning coal; Rashbam suggests he'd lost fluency in Egyptian.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of 3:11 (the quotation stops at 'Pharaoh', where JPS continues with ', and that I should bring forth…'), 3:12, 4:10, 4:11.
Exodus Rabbah 1:26 (the coal) and Rashbam on 4:10 (lost fluency): confirm.
Humility of Moses (Numbers 12:3) in howItsDone: paraphrased, confirm.
Disability sensitivity: the script avoids calling his speech a defect and says the weakness stays; confirm tone.

Editor review: hook no longer tells the listener what has happened to them ('You've probably had this happen'); unsourced superlative 'the greatest prophet in Jewish tradition' replaced with Deuteronomy 34:10's own claim (added to sources).
